episodes.168094: Clusters of strong to severe thunderstorms accompanied a cold front as it moved southeast across southeast Missouri. The lack of stronger vertical wind shear limited storm organization, favoring a predominantly multicellular storm mode. Even so, a few large hail events and a damaging downburst were reported.
episodes.168777: A mesoscale convective system moved across the Mid-South. This feature interacted with a remnant outflow boundary resulting in thunderstorm development. Damaging wind, large hail, and heavy rain were reported across the Mid-South.
episodes.168778: A mesoscale convective system moved across the Mid-South. This feature interacted with a remnant outflow boundary resulting in thunderstorm development. Damaging wind, large hail, and heavy rain were reported across the Mid-South.

episodes.168781: A mesoscale convective system moved across the Mid-South. This feature interacted with a remnant outflow boundary resulting in thunderstorm development. Damaging wind, large hail, and heavy rain were reported across the Mid-South.
episodes.168855: Slow-moving storms fired in the late afternoon and evening hours of May 14th in a pattern of high moisture, weak overall flow,  and weak vorticity advection.  The slow storm movement resulted in localized heavy rainfall.  One instance of flash flooding was noted in Washington County.
episodes.168913: A weak pressure pattern was across the local area with a ridge across the western Atlantic and a mid/upper level across the Carolinas to Florida panhandle with weak SW flow aloft over the local area. Mid level temps warmed, but mid level lapse rates were modest around 6.7 degC/km with surface based CAPE increasing to near 2500 J/kg in the afternoon with surface dew pts near 70 degF. Shear was not impressive, but neared 15-25 kts across NE FL in the afternoon which enabled some stronger cells to form with gusty wind, hail and weak tornado potential.
episodes.169019: Isolated thunderstorms developed along the Altamaha River in the early afternoon hours. One thunderstorm moved into Long County and produced large hail.
episodes.169079: Storms developed along a weak frontal boundary across the southern half of the forecast area. Some of the storms became severe with several reports of large hail and damaging winds.
episodes.169080: Storms developed along a weak frontal boundary across the southern half of the forecast area. Some of the storms became severe with several reports of large hail and damaging winds.
episodes.169083: As a cold front moved through the region, it triggered showers and storms. Some of the storms became severe with reports of damaging winds, large hail and a brief tornado.
episodes.169084: As a cold front moved through the region, it triggered showers and storms. Some of the storms became severe with reports of damaging winds, large hail and a brief tornado.
episodes.169368: A weak trough contributed to scattered showers and thunderstorms across the area.  The atmosphere was just unstable enough for a couple of severe weather reports.
episodes.169412: Scattered severe storms affected the region during the overnight into the morning hours of May 15th, 2022.  Most of the severe events were around one inch, however a few hail stone reports up to 1.5 inches in diameter were noted.
episodes.169427: Isolated severe thunderstorms develop during the early morning hours of May 15th, producing large hail and damaging winds over portions of south central Nebraska. Activity initially developed along and north of Interstate 80 across Dawson and Buffalo Counties between 1AM and 2AM CDT. Initial thunderstorms evolved into a few small clusters as they moved southeast and produced marginally severe hail up to quarter size, and severe wind gusts of 60 to 65 MPH. Overall, this was a minor event by local severe weather standards.
episodes.169562: Thunderstorms moving through Lake St. Clair and St. Clair River produced wind gusts between 40-50 mph.
episodes.169585: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms developed across west central Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 14th. The strongest storms produced large hail to half dollar size. Isolated strong to severe thunderstorms redeveloped late in the evening across northwestern Arkansas. Moderately strong instability combined with strong deep layer wind shear promoted the development of a supercell in Washington County, which produced large hail up to ping pong ball size.||Thunderstorms that developed across northeastern Kansas during the early morning hours of the 15th, moved southeast across portions of northwestern Arkansas during the afternoon. Additional thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon and evening near the outflow boundary from these storms. The strongest storms produced large hail up to quarter size and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.169586: Scattered strong to severe thunderstorms developed near an outflow boundary across northeastern Oklahoma during the early morning hours of the 15th. The strongest thunderstorms produced large hail up to ping pong ball size. Additional strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon and evening hours, along a southward-moving outflow boundary from earlier thunderstorms that moved through southwestern Missouri and northwestern Arkansas. The atmosphere along and south of this outflow boundary in eastern Oklahoma had become very unstable by the afternoon, and combined with strong deep layer wind shear across the area, an environment supportive of supercells was in place as the storms developed. Several supercells moved across the region, producing large hail up to softball size.
episodes.169622: Strong to severe storms moved southeastward from northwest Missouri into the Ozarks during the morning and early afternoon of the 15th. The strongest storms within this storm complex produced wind gusts over 60 mph and caused damage to trees, powerlines and roofs mainly over southwest Missouri from Mount Vernon to Table Rock Lake.
episodes.169668: Several supercells moved southward out Kansas during the evening of the 14th, with multiple large hail reports received, some up to the size of tennis balls., along with a few reports of severe wind gusts.
episodes.169672: An outflow boundary moving into an extremely unstable airmass sparked multiple supercell thunderstorms with very large hail close to softball sized and strong damaging wind gusts.
episodes.169724: Multiple clusters of thunderstorms developed and moved through central and northeast KS during the morning of 5/15 producing severe winds and large hail.
episodes.169787: A line of severe thunderstorms moved through southeast Arkansas on the evening of May 15th. This line of storms produced widespread damaging winds with numerous trees downed, including several that fell onto structures and vehicles. Outflow from these thunderstorms created a dust storm across southeast Arkansas as visibilities dropped to one quarter of a mile before the rain started.
episodes.169792: A line of severe thunderstorms moved through portions of western and central Mississippi on the evening of May 15th. Widespread damaging winds downed numerous trees and power lines with several trees falling onto structures and vehicles. Outflow from these thunderstorms created a dust storm across the Mississippi Delta as visibilities dropped to one quarter of a mile before the rain started.  In addition, a separate cluster of storms in eastern Mississippi produced scattered wind damage across Noxubee County.
episodes.169795: A multi-cluster batch of showers and thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall that resulted in multiple flash flood reports and also produced a few damaging wind reports across eastern New York during the afternoon and evening hours of May 15, 2022.
episodes.169841: For much of the state, May 13th was the end of the heatwave as a cold front moved into the area and showers and thunderstorms developed. Thunderstorms were most widespread on the 15th with several reports of hail as large as golf balls and numerous wind damage reports. A wind gust of 58 mph was recorded at the Jacksonville/LR Air Force Base.||Some relief (cooler air) came on the 15th in the form of a cold front. At the same time, there were strong to severe storms ahead of the front.  Storms were sure to thrive given an enormous amount of energy in place. Models showed a line of storms traversing the region from northwest to southeast during the afternoon, and these were expected to unleash strong to damaging winds. Updrafts into some storms were likely to be powerful enough to suspend hailstones aloft, and allow them to grow. So, very large hail was possible. There were already a few hailstorms on the 14th, with lime size hail at Jasper (Newton County), and golf ball size hail at Harrison (Boone County). Tornadoes were much less likely because steering winds were generally weak (30 knots or less), and there was not much shear.||Between 1100 am and 1200 pm CST, a large cluster of storms arrived from Missouri. Ahead of the cluster, isolated to scattered storms erupted mainly north and west of Little Rock (Pulaski County). Golf ball size hail was reported at Boxley (Newton County) and the west side of Russellville (Pope County). There was half dollar size hail at London and just north of Russellville (both in Pope County), and quarter size stones at Chickalah (Yell County), Nimrod (Perry County), and Paris (Logan County).||As the afternoon progressed, the cluster of storms worked from northwest into central and southeast Arkansas. Numerous trees and power lines were downed, with some trees on houses. At least 50,000 power outages were noted at one point. At Russellville (Pope County), a tree fell on a vehicle, and two people had to be extricated and taken to the hospital. A tree also came down on a travel trailer close to Hazen (Prairie County). Fallen trees blocked Highway 7 near Fourche Junction (Perry County), Highway 46 at Sheridan (Grant County), and Highway 54 at Sulphur Springs (Jefferson County). Roads were blocked by trees at a campground northeast of Fifty Six (Stone County). A roof was blown off of a storage building west of Hot Springs (Garland County).||There was a 58 mph gust at the Little Rock Air Force Base (Pulaski County), a 56 mph gust at McCreanor (Lonoke County), a 55 mph gust at Little Rock National Airport (Pulaski County), and a 54 mph gust at the Stuttgart Airport in Fairmount (Prairie County).
episodes.169948: Early on the morning of May 15, 2022 a complex of storms moved through the Kansas City metro, causing scattered wind damage. Most of the wind gusts were in the 60 to 70 mph range, and caused relatively minor damage.
episodes.169949: Early on the morning of May 15, 2022 a complex of storms moved through the Kansas City metro, causing scattered wind damage. Most of the wind gusts were in the 60 to 70 mph range, and caused relatively minor damage.
episodes.170038: A weak frontal boundary began to develop across southeast Louisiana and the Mississippi Gulf Coast. Convergence along this boundary became the focus for a few thunderstoms to develop. The evening upper air sounding at LIX indicated mid level temperatures cool enough to support severe thunderstorms with hail.
episodes.170039: The region was under the influence of northwest flow in the upper levels. More importantly, the mid levels cooled and low levels warmed quite a bit compared to previous days. That combination resulted in steep lapse rates, a very unstable mid level environment. This was especially so over coastal locations of the local area, multiple storms produced severe thunderstorm winds.
episodes.170040: The region was under the influence of northwest flow in the upper levels. More importantly, the mid levels cooled and low levels warmed quite a bit compared to previous days. That combination resulted in steep lapse rates, a very unstable mid level environment. This was especially so over coastal locations of the local area, multiple storms produced very large hail.
episodes.170041: The region was under the influence of northwest flow in the upper levels. More importantly, the mid levels cooled and low levels warmed quite a bit compared to previous days. episodes.170057: A cold front interacting with a seasonably warm and moist airmass triggered scattered strong thunderstorms across east-central and southeast Illinois during the afternoon and early evening of May 15th.  Hail as large as nickels was reported in Newman in Douglas County.
episodes.170094: Several weak upper level impulses provided the lift for scattered strong to severe thunderstorms to develop during the heating of the day on May 15th.  Instability parameters were higher than normal for mid May due to above normal temperatures and surface moisture.
episodes.170162: An upper level shortwave trough lifting northeast across the region produced isolated thunderstorms across northeast Oregon in the afternoon of May 15th. At least one of these thunderstorms was strong enough to produce severe hail as it crossed I-84 several miles east of Pendleton, Or.
episodes.170171: A series of short waves affected the region during the 14th and 15th producing rounds of storms. An isolated thunderstorm became severe on both days.

episodes.170281: An upper level trough over the eastern Gulf of Mexico provided enough instability to trigger showers and thunderstorms over the near shore Atlantic waters.
episodes.170282: An upper level trough over the eastern Gulf of Mexico and sea breezes combined to produce scattered strong to severe thunderstorms over western sections of Miami-Dade and Broward counties.
episodes.170325: Marginal boundary layer moisture along combined with sufficient daytime warming was enough to generate mainly high based thunderstorms. Ample shear of over 30 kts and CAPE values over 1000 J/kg contributed to a number of nickel to quarter sized hail reports.
episodes.170495: Scattered showers and thunderstorms affected Middle Tennessee during the afternoon and evening hours on May 14, with a few reports of large hail and wind damage.
episodes.174576: A stationary front produced heavy showers and flash flooding on May 13 and May 15 to May 17.
